sections.name: The company
sections.guide: You're trying to understand what they're building, how far along it is, and what the cofounders want out of it. Approach it like a friend asking what they're working on: let them tell the story, and pick up details as they come. The basics are mostly setup. Don't stay on this section too long, or it'll feel like they aren't making progress at the start. A good conversation here ends with a clear picture of the company, its legal status or a plan for it, and each cofounder's ambition.

checklist.item: Company name
One-line description
Incorporated yet or not
Formation date
checklist.notes: Only if they're incorporated; skip it otherwise.

checklist.item: Entity type
checklist.notes: Some people get stuck here. Help them with what's common for startups like theirs, such as a Delaware C-Corp if they plan to raise money, rather than guessing for them.

checklist.item: State of incorporation
checklist.notes: If they haven't incorporated yet, ask where they plan to.

checklist.item: Mailing address for notices

sections.name: The cofounders
sections.guide: You're trying to understand who the cofounders are and how they work together. This is where you learn everyone's names. A good conversation here ends with a clear picture of who each cofounder is, what they do, when they started, and anything outside the company that could matter.

checklist.item: Who the cofounders are
checklist.notes: Be precise about who counts. A cofounder works on the company full-time and will typically hold more than 10% of the equity, which is different from founding team members like founding engineers; employees, advisors and contractors don't count. If someone isn't full-time, they aren't a cofounder for this agreement: explain that gently and suggest they come on as an advisor or early employee instead.

checklist.item: How they met and how long they've known each other
checklist.notes: It doesn't go into the agreement, but it tells you how much trust and history there is. Listen for a personal relationship, like family, a partner, or close friends. That's common and fine, but it means taking extra care later with how disagreements and departures are handled, so keep it in mind.

checklist.item: Each cofounder's legal name
Each cofounder's email
checklist.notes: Each one must be different.

checklist.item: Each cofounder's title
checklist.notes: Titles may overlap.

checklist.item: What each cofounder owns day to day
checklist.notes: Roles can overlap, but if two cofounders both claim the same area, ask who has the final call, since that comes back when you cover decisions.

checklist.item: Who the CEO is
checklist.notes: Exactly one. If they haven't settled it, help them think it through rather than picking for them.

checklist.item: Each cofounder's start date
checklist.notes: If one cofounder started earlier, ask whether that head start should count toward their vesting.

checklist.item: Each cofounder's outside work
checklist.notes: Other projects, or advising other companies. Note each one, or that there is none.

checklist.item: Whether outside work is allowed
checklist.notes: A sensible default is that outside work is fine if it doesn't compete and is disclosed.

checklist.item: Existing conflicts of interest
checklist.notes: A connection to anything the company might do business with, like hiring a relative or buying from a company a cofounder owns. Note each one, or that there is none.

checklist.item: How conflicts of interest are handled
checklist.notes: Disclosed and approved, or disclosed only. A sensible default is that conflicts are disclosed in writing and approved by the other cofounders.

sections.name: Ownership and vesting
sections.guide: You're trying to understand how the cofounders plan to split equity. It's one of the most sensitive topics, and people who haven't done this before will have questions. Stay neutral. A good conversation here ends with a split everyone can explain, a vesting schedule that fits how long each person is committing, and a clear plan for leave and a sale.

checklist.item: Each cofounder's equity percentage
checklist.notes: Start by finding out whether they've already agreed on a split. Listen for hesitation like "I guess" or "I think he's fine with it." If you hear it, gently walk through the factors below, and mark this revisit if the respondent isn't sure the others agree. If they haven't decided, help them get there. Reflect back what you already know, like who started first and who built what. Ask whether anyone is putting in money or bringing something hard to replace, like code, key customers, or expertise the company depends on. Equal splits are common when contributions are similar, but don't let them land on 50/50 without thinking about it. A different split should rest on a clear, lasting difference, not on who had the idea, and vesting protects everyone if the split turns out to be wrong. Then ask what split feels right. If they still can't decide, note a tentative split and mark this revisit, since the agreement can't be finished without one. The percentages total 100% or less; if less, ask what the rest is for.

checklist.item: Why the split is what it is
checklist.notes: Note the reasoning in their own words. If anyone wants to revisit the split later, this is the reference point.

checklist.item: Vesting schedule length
checklist.notes: Explain vesting simply: each cofounder earns their shares over time, so someone who leaves early doesn't walk away with a full stake. The standard is four years (48 months) with a one-year cliff, vesting monthly after that. Offer it as the default, and recommend it strongly even if they lean toward something else.

checklist.item: Vesting cliff
checklist.notes: Standard is 12 months. It must be shorter than the schedule.

checklist.item: How often shares vest after the cliff
checklist.notes: Monthly or quarterly. Standard is monthly.

checklist.item: Each cofounder's vesting start date
checklist.notes: Use the start dates from the cofounders section. If a cofounder's earlier work should count, start their vesting from when they started. Otherwise, use the formation date if the company is incorporated, or the signing date if it isn't. Don't credit the same work twice by also giving them shares up front.

checklist.item: Vesting during extended leave
checklist.notes: Like parental or medical leave: vesting continues or pauses. The default is that vesting continues for the first 30 days, then pauses until they return.

checklist.item: What happens to unvested shares if the company is sold
checklist.notes: None, single-trigger or double-trigger. Unvested shares can vest right away on a sale (single-trigger), or only if the cofounder is let go or their role is cut after the sale (double-trigger). Buyers generally prefer double-trigger because it keeps the team in place. Recommend double-trigger unless they have a reason to want something else. Use standard definitions of "let go" and "role cut," and don't negotiate them in conversation.

checklist.item: How much of the unvested shares vest on a sale
checklist.notes: Skip it if nothing vests on a sale. The default is full acceleration (100%).

checklist.item: How long after a sale double-trigger applies
checklist.notes: Only for double-trigger; skip it otherwise. The default is 12 months after the sale.

checklist.item: Whether everyone goes along with a sale the majority agrees to
checklist.notes: Ask whether everyone should go along with a sale if the cofounders holding most of the shares agree to it. This is called drag-along, and it stops one holdout from blocking a sale. The default is yes. Note it as their intent, since the formal terms come later in other documents.

sections.name: Decisions and governance
sections.guide: You're trying to understand how the cofounders make decisions together. Most have never talked about this in detail, because so far they've agreed on everything. Your job is to help them decide now, while it's easy, how they'll handle the moments when they don't. Start with the big decisions, then everyday ones, then deadlocks, then fundraising. A good conversation here ends with clear answers on what needs everyone, who decides day to day, what happens when they can't agree, and who handles fundraising.

checklist.item: A real disagreement they've had and how it got resolved
checklist.notes: A good way into this section. It doesn't go into the agreement, but it shows you how they actually work together and makes the rules that follow feel grounded rather than hypothetical. If they say they never disagree, ask about a decision coming up where they might see things differently.

checklist.item: Decisions every cofounder must agree to
checklist.notes: Ask which decisions feel important enough that every cofounder should have to agree. Common ones are selling or merging the company, raising money or issuing new shares, adding a cofounder, granting equity, major pivots, large contracts, and taking on significant debt. Offer these as suggestions, not a checklist. Removing a cofounder shouldn't be on the list, because that person could block it.

checklist.item: Whether votes are equal or weighted by ownership
checklist.notes: Equal is most common between cofounders, and it's the default.

checklist.item: Who gets the final call on everyday decisions when they're split
checklist.notes: The CEO, by area, or no one. Usually it's the CEO, which is the default. Some teams split authority by area, like the CTO deciding technical questions. With two cofounders and equal votes, every disagreement is a tie, so make sure they've chosen a tie-break, or that they understand every split will go to the deadlock process.

checklist.item: Which cofounder decides each area
checklist.notes: Only if they split authority by area; skip it otherwise. Map each area to a cofounder using what you learned about roles, and make clear the big decisions still need everyone.

checklist.item: What happens when they're stuck on something big
checklist.notes: The default is mediation with a neutral third party, and if that doesn't work, nothing changes and the proposed action doesn't happen. Some teams would rather name a trusted advisor or board member to decide. If the cofounders have a personal relationship, recommend mediation. For two-cofounder teams, mention that a trusted advisor is the only way to actually break a deadlock rather than leave it standing, which matters later if one of them ever needs to be removed.

checklist.item: The trusted advisor's name
checklist.notes: Only if a trusted advisor decides deadlocks; skip it otherwise.

checklist.item: Who leads conversations with investors
Who signs the funding documents
checklist.notes: The default is the CEO.

sections.name: Money
sections.guide: You're trying to understand the money between the cofounders and the company. Most early cofounders haven't put in much yet, so keep this short and don't make it feel like an audit. A good conversation here ends with all the money between the cofounders and the company recorded, any personal guarantees known, pay settled, and a spending limit in place.

checklist.item: Money any cofounder has put into company costs
checklist.notes: Ask whether anyone has paid for company costs out of pocket, like contractors, software, or incorporation fees, and move on quickly if not. If they have, find out who paid, how much, and whether they want it repaid as a loan (with its terms), counted toward their equity, reimbursed as an expense, or left as a contribution. If any of it should count toward equity, go back to the equity split and make sure it still reflects that.

checklist.item: Personal guarantees for the company
checklist.notes: Anything a cofounder has personally guaranteed, like an office lease, a loan, or a credit card: who, what, and how much. Note that there are none if so.

checklist.item: What the company does about those guarantees
checklist.notes: Only if there are any; skip it otherwise. The default is that the company works to release the guarantor as soon as it can.

checklist.item: Whether any cofounder is paid now or soon
checklist.notes: Most early cofounders aren't.

checklist.item: Each paid cofounder's salary
checklist.notes: Only if someone is paid; skip it otherwise.

checklist.item: Deferred salary for the others
checklist.notes: If one cofounder needs pay before the others, ask whether the rest should get deferred salary, and how it builds up. That evens things out without touching the equity split. If someone thinks the pay difference should change the split, mark the equity percentage item revisit with a note, since all the cofounders should decide that together.

checklist.item: When deferred salary is paid out
checklist.notes: Only if there's deferred salary; skip it otherwise. The default is at the first priced round or a sale, whichever comes first.

checklist.item: How much one cofounder can spend without checking with the others
checklist.notes: Most early teams haven't set a limit, and having one avoids arguments. If they have no view, suggest $1,000 per purchase.

checklist.item: Whether the spending limit is per purchase or per month
How expenses are reimbursed
checklist.notes: The default is that normal business expenses are reimbursed with receipts.

sections.name: What you built
sections.guide: You're trying to make sure the company owns what it's built on. Most of this has standard answers, so lean on the defaults and keep it short. A good conversation here ends with everything the company uses belonging to it, any employer agreements known or marked to revisit, and a clear answer on who controls the company's accounts.

checklist.item: What the company uses that was made before it existed
checklist.notes: Like code, designs, a prototype, a domain, a brand, or research. For each one, note what it is and who made it. The default is that anything the company uses is assigned to it. If anything was made with someone who isn't a cofounder, like a friend at a hackathon, that person would need to sign their rights over. Note that there is nothing if so.

checklist.item: Anything a cofounder keeps
checklist.notes: The default is nothing: everything the company uses is assigned to it. If a cofounder wants to keep something the company depends on, mark this revisit with a note, because the company would then need permission to keep using it.

checklist.item: Each cofounder's agreements with past or current employers
checklist.notes: Anything they signed about inventions, side projects, or non-competes. If it came up in the cofounders section, confirm it instead of asking again. Building while employed is the most common way a startup's ownership of its own code gets challenged.

checklist.item: Who controls the company's accounts
checklist.notes: The domain, code repositories, social accounts, and cloud services. The default is that they're held in the company's name with more than one cofounder having access, because accounts on someone's personal login are hard to recover if that person leaves.

sections.name: When things change
sections.guide: You're trying to agree on what happens when things change: a cofounder underperforming, leaving, being asked to leave, dying, or becoming unable to work, and what happens if the company shuts down. It's the hardest part of the conversation. Tell them every good agreement covers these situations, so it doesn't sound like you expect them to happen. Most people want this part done quickly, and the standard answers are standard for good reasons, so lean on them. A good conversation here ends with a clear process for performance, leaving, removal, and incapacity, the post-departure restrictions set, and a plan for the company's assets if it closes.

checklist.item: What not pulling their weight would look like
checklist.notes: Use each cofounder's role and their full-time commitment as the baseline.

checklist.item: What happens when a cofounder underperforms
checklist.notes: The default is a written warning and a plan to fix it before anything more serious, like a role change or removal. Agreeing on this now gives them a fair process to point to instead of an argument.

checklist.item: How long an underperforming cofounder has to improve
checklist.notes: The default is 30 days.

checklist.item: Notice a cofounder gives before leaving
checklist.notes: The default is 30 days, with their work handed off during that time. Vesting continues through the notice period and stops when it ends.

checklist.item: What happens to a departing cofounder's vested shares
checklist.notes: The standard is that unvested shares go back to the company at what the cofounder paid for them. For vested shares: no buyback, an optional buyback, or a required buyback, at fair market value. The default is that the company has the option, but not the obligation, to buy them back. Some teams prefer the company always buy them back, so former cofounders don't stay on as shareholders. If the respondent says the reason for leaving should matter, mark this revisit with a note.

checklist.item: How long the company has to buy back vested shares
checklist.notes: The default is 90 days.

checklist.item: How a cofounder could be asked to leave
checklist.notes: The default is that the other cofounders decide together, or the board decides by majority, and the cofounder in question doesn't vote. With only two cofounders, neither can remove the other without agreement, so tell them that plainly. If they chose mediation for deadlocks, a failed mediation means nothing changes, so in practice neither can be removed, even after the performance process runs its course. If they want removal to be possible, they'd need a trusted advisor to break the deadlock.

checklist.item: Vested shares if a cofounder dies or becomes permanently unable to work
checklist.notes: Be gentle with this one. Unvested shares go back to the company. For vested shares: an optional buyback, a required buyback, or they pass to the estate. The default is that the company can buy them back from the estate at fair market value.

checklist.item: Whether any unvested shares vest if a cofounder dies or becomes unable to work
checklist.notes: The default is none.

checklist.item: Not competing after leaving
checklist.notes: The default is no competing for 12 months where that's allowed. Non-competes are often unenforceable in some states, including California. If any cofounder lives in one of those states, leave the non-compete out for everyone rather than applying it unevenly, and suggest they confirm with a lawyer.

checklist.item: Not recruiting the company's employees or customers after leaving
checklist.notes: The default is 12 months.

checklist.item: Not criticizing each other or the company publicly after a split
checklist.notes: The default is yes, applied to all of them equally.

checklist.item: What happens to the company's IP and accounts if it shuts down
checklist.notes: The IP, code, and accounts. The default is that everything stays with the company until it's wound up.

checklist.item: Whether a cofounder can restart the idea after a shutdown
checklist.notes: If so, note who and on what terms.

checklist.item: What happens to the company's name and brand if it shuts down
checklist.notes: The default is that they stay with the company, but some teams let a named cofounder keep them or agree to sell them.

sections.name: Wrap-up
sections.guide: You're trying to settle the last few terms that keep the agreement working over time. The hard conversations are done, so keep this quick. A good conversation here ends with a way to resolve disputes, a governing state, and a plan for reviewing and amending the agreement.

checklist.item: How disputes about the agreement are resolved
checklist.notes: Make clear this is different from the deadlock process in the governance section, which covers business decisions. This one covers disagreements about what the agreement means or whether someone kept to it. The default is mediation first, then binding arbitration if that fails. Explain that arbitration is usually faster and more private than court, but harder to appeal. Don't say whether arbitration is enforceable in their situation; suggest a lawyer instead.

checklist.item: Which state's law governs the agreement
checklist.notes: Confirm it. The default is the state of incorporation, or the state they plan to incorporate in if they haven't yet.

checklist.item: How often they review the agreement
checklist.notes: Every 3, 6 or 12 months. Companies change fast early on, so the default is once a year.

checklist.item: Whether any cofounder can request a review sooner
checklist.notes: The default is yes.

checklist.item: How the agreement gets changed
checklist.notes: Confirm it. The default is that every current cofounder agrees in writing.
